title: Paint Canvas — The PNG Is the Canvas — SnapDOM Labs
text:
⌕ Overview All labs Live demos Stop motion Paint on a capture Capture stages Target range WebGL Live mirror Seamless DOM Shattered capture Labs / Live demos / Paint on a capture Labs Experiment The PNG is the canvas The drawing surface is an backed by an SVG stroke layer. A SnapDOM plugin saves the clone from the last capture and adds each stroke to it, then exports the next PNG. SnapDOM uses Canvas internally for that raster export. TL;DR The plugin's afterRender hook saves the clone; afterClone swaps it back in on the next call and appends the newest stroke. Successive PNG exports preserve the accumulated drawing. What you're looking at Pick a color and brush size, then drag across the board. What looks like a normal painting widget is actually a single hidden
holding an empty SVG layer, plus an that gets replaced every time SnapDOM re-renders it. There is no persistent bitmap buffer anywhere in the page's own code — the persistence lives entirely inside the plugin. Try it Draw on the board below. The line under your cursor is a local SVG path with zero SnapDOM involvement — it never waits on a capture. Underneath, roughly every 120ms, that same stroke gets folded into the plugin's saved clone and re-exported as a real PNG. Brush Clear Download painting How it works A hidden source element, never the visible board A 420×420
off-screen holds one empty replaces the board's picture The resulting PNG is inserted directly into the board. The download button just points at that same .src — no second capture needed. Why this needed a plugin SnapDOM v3.x.x can reuse eligible captures, but the accumulated drawing here belongs to the plugin. On each stroke, the plugin replaces the new clone with its saved clone and adds the latest mark. Its stateful hooks run on fresh captures. The afterClone and afterRender hooks share the plugin closure. afterClone adds the new mark to savedClone ; afterRender saves the resulting tree for the next call. The plugin owns this drawing state independently of capture reuse. Copy-paste example The plugin factory — swap in your own persistence logic and this pattern works for any "keep building on the last capture" use case, not just painting: function createPaintPlugin (sourceEl) { let savedClone = null let skipNext = false let pendingStroke = null function makePath (stroke) { const path = document.createElementNS('http://www.w3.org/2000/svg', 'path') path.setAttribute('data-stroke-id', stroke.id) path.setAttribute('d', stroke.d) path.setAttribute('fill', 'none') path.setAttribute('stroke', stroke.color) path.setAttribute('stroke-width', stroke.size) path.setAttribute('stroke-linecap', 'round') path.setAttribute('stroke-linejoin', 'round') return path } return { name: 'paint', recordStroke (stroke) { pendingStroke = stroke }, afterClone (ctx) { if (skipNext) { skipNext = false; pendingStroke = null; return } if (savedClone) ctx.clone = savedClone.cloneNode(true) if (!pendingStroke) return const layer = ctx.clone.querySelector('.strokes') const existing = layer.querySelector(`[data-stroke-id="${pendingStroke.id}"]`) if (existing) existing.setAttribute('d', pendingStroke.d) else layer.append(makePath(pendingStroke)) }, afterRender (ctx) { savedClone = ctx.clone.cloneNode(true) pendingStroke = null }, clear () { skipNext = true } } } And the usage — capture again on every stroke update, plugin included: const plugin = createPaintPlugin(canvasSource) async function render (stroke) { if (stroke) plugin.recordStroke(stroke) const img = await snapdom.toPng(canvasSource, { plugins: [plugin] }) board.replaceChildren(img) } // on clear: plugin.clear() then render() again — skipNext lets SnapDOM // clone the pristine live element once, instead of hand-building an // empty replacement clone that might miss pipeline setup. stroke recordStroke() snapdom.toPng() afterClone (restore + append) afterRender (checkpoint) Limits and things to watch Every stroke update is a full SnapDOM capture, so the render loop is throttled (120ms here) rather than firing on every pointermove — captures aren't free, and a paint app that tries to snapshot on every mouse event will fall behind. The visible "live" path is what keeps the drawing feeling instant while the real PNG catches up underneath. The skipNext flag matters more than it looks: without it, clear() would need to hand-build an empty clone instead of letting SnapDOM's own cloning pipeline produce one, and any pipeline behavior added later (pseudo-elements, SVG defs inlining, etc.) would silently stop applying to the very first render after a clear. title: WebGL Shatter — A Capture, Shattered — SnapDOM Labs
text: ⌕ Overview All labs Live demos Stop motion Paint on a capture Capture stages Target range WebGL Live mirror Seamless DOM Shattered capture Labs / WebGL / Shattered capture Labs Experiment A capture, shattered Five WebGL shaders, one starting point: a SnapDOM capture of a live, editable card, turned into a WebGL texture. Nothing here exists without rasterizing the DOM first. TL;DR A custom defineExports plugin ( shatterExport ) adds a custom export type — result.toShatter() — that isn't a thin wrapper around toPng / toCanvas . It reuses the core canvas exporter internally via the "silent" ctx.exports.canvas() facade (no re-triggered beforeExport / afterExport hooks), then slices that canvas into a grid of small canvases for the physics simulation to grab as WebGL textures. The other four effects — ripple, glitch, dissolve, metal — don't need the plugin at all: they just take the whole card as one texture via plain snapdom.toCanvas() . What you're looking at The card's heading and paragraph are contenteditable — editable HTML. Whatever you type is what ends up baked into the WebGL texture, because SnapDOM captures the card exactly as it currently renders: your text, your font metrics, the gradient, the shadow. Edit the copy, then apply an effect, and you're watching your own words get shattered, rippled, or dissolved. Try it Edit the card, pick an effect, hit Shatter (the button relabels itself per effect). Ripple, Glitch, and Dissolve settle or complete on their own — well, Dissolve needs a manual Reset since it ends empty. Metal stays interactive, tracking your pointer, until you exit it. Shatter Ripple Glitch Dissolve Metal Live DOM Try me! This text is genuinely editable HTML. SnapDOM captures it exactly as it renders — font, gradient, shadow — and turns it into a WebGL texture. 100% SnapDOM Shatter Reset Edit the card's text before applying an effect — you'll see your own text, not a canned image. How it works Ripple, Glitch, Dissolve, Metal: one texture, one shader snapdom.toCanvas(card, { scale: 2 }) captures the card once as a single canvas. That canvas becomes a WebGL texture via texImage2D , and a per-effect fragment shader distorts or reveals it over a fixed duration — or, for Metal, indefinitely while tracking pointer position. The card hides while the effect plays The card's CSS visibility is set to hidden right after the texture is captured, and restored once the effect finishes — except Metal, which stays hidden and interactive until you explicitly exit it. Shatter needs more than one texture The shatterExport plugin's defineExports(ctx) returns a shatter export function. Calling result.toShatter({ cols, rows }) first gets a canvas via ctx.exports.canvas(opts) — the same core canvas exporter, called directly, bypassing the plugin pipeline's own hook re-runs. That canvas is sliced into a grid The canvas is cut into cols × rows small canvases with drawImage , each one becoming its own WebGL texture positioned at its origin cell. Physics takes over Each piece gets a random launch velocity and rotation on spawn; gravity is applied every frame, and pieces fade out until none are left. Why this needed a plugin SnapDOM's built-in exports — toPng , toCanvas , toSvg , toBlob — all return one complete image. There's no option to get back "the same capture, pre-sliced into N pieces," because slicing into tiles is a shatter-effect concern, not a general capture concern. defineExports is exactly the seam SnapDOM exposes for adding an export shape that doesn't exist in core. And because the new shatter export still needs ordinary canvas pixels underneath it, it calls back into the "silent" ctx.exports.{img,svg,canvas,blob,png,jpeg,webp} facade, which reuses the core exporter functions directly without re-running the plugin's own beforeExport / afterExport hooks — avoiding infinite recursion and duplicate hook firing. The other four effects deliberately don't use a plugin at all, and that's the point: most creative uses of a SnapDOM capture don't need one. defineExports is for the narrower case of inventing a new output shape , not a substitute for reaching for toCanvas() first. Copy-paste example The plugin factory — cols / rows control how fine the grid is: function shatterExport (options = {}) { const { cols: defaultCols = 14, rows: defaultRows = 9 } = options return { name: 'shatter', defineExports (ctx) { return { shatter: async (_ctx2, opts = {}) => { const cols = opts.cols || defaultCols const rows = opts.rows || defaultRows // Reuse the core canvas exporter directly — this does NOT // re-run beforeExport/afterExport, so it's safe to call from // inside another export. const canvas = await ctx.exports.canvas(opts) const pw = canvas.width / cols const ph = canvas.height / rows const pieces = [] for (let ry = 0; ry Usage — the plugin is local to this one capture, and toShatter() shows up as a method on the result alongside the built-in toPng / toCanvas : const result = await snapdom(card, { plugins: [shatterExport({ cols: 16, rows: 11 })] }) const { pieces } = await result.toShatter() // pieces[i] = { u, v, du, dv, canvas } — grid position (0..1) plus a // small <canvas>, ready to hand to texImage2D as its own WebGL texture The other four effects skip the plugin entirely — one capture, one texture: const canvas = await snapdom.toCanvas(card, { scale: 2 }) const tex = makeTexture(canvas) // gl.texImage2D(..., canvas) card snapdom(plugins) result.toShatter() ctx.exports.canvas() slice into pieces WebGL textures Limits and things to watch The ctx.exports.canvas() facade is documented in PLUGIN_SPEC.md . It lets a custom exporter reuse core Canvas output without invoking its own export hooks again. Splitting this capture into a 16×11 grid creates 176 pieces; finer grids add draw calls, textures and memory. title: Stop Motion — You Choose the Frames — SnapDOM Labs
text: ⌕ Overview All labs Live demos Stop motion Paint on a capture Capture stages Target range WebGL Live mirror Seamless DOM Shattered capture Labs / Live demos / Stop motion Labs Experiment You choose the frames No continuous sampling here. You pose an actor, press the shutter, and move on — the sequence is exactly the poses you decided were worth keeping, like a physical stop-motion rig. TL;DR A tiny plugin's afterRender hook fires once per capture and hands back ctx.dataURL . Nothing accumulates onto a saved clone — unlike the paint-canvas and target-range labs, each capture here is fully independent. The plugin's only job is to collect the dataURLs you explicitly ask for into an ordered array; the player decides the playback rhythm afterward. What you're looking at The three sliders position and rotate an actor sprite on a small stage. Nothing you do with them triggers a capture — they just change CSS on a live element. Pressing Capture pose runs one SnapDOM capture of that stage and appends the result to a filmstrip. Pressing Play flips through the filmstrip at a fixed interval, like a flipbook. Try it Drag the sliders to pose the actor, capture a few poses from different positions, then hit play. Every thumbnail in the filmstrip below is a separate, independent SVG snapshot — there's no shared state between them. Horizontal Vertical Rotation + Capture pose Play Capture at least two poses. How it works The plugin factory closes over a counter frameCollector(onFrame) returns a plugin holding a private index variable — nothing else. It persists the frame count, but no clone or DOM reference. Moving a slider never captures anything Dragging Horizontal, Vertical, or Rotation just updates inline styles and a CSS custom property on the live #actor element. SnapDOM is not involved yet. Capture pose runs one real capture The button calls snapdom(poseScene, { plugins: [collector] }) against the current, live state of the stage — whatever pose the sliders are showing right now. afterRender fires with the finished context Once SnapDOM renders the SVG, the plugin's afterRender(ctx) hook runs, increments its counter, and calls back with { index, url: ctx.dataURL } . The page pushes the URL into an array capturedFrames.push(frame.url) , plus a thumbnail appended to the filmstrip. The plugin doesn't know or care that a filmstrip exists — it just handed the URL to a callback. Play iterates the array on a timer Pressing Play walks capturedFrames for a few loops, swapping .src on an interval. The plugin is done by this point — playback is pure application code. Why this needed a plugin Contrast this with the accumulation pattern in the paint-canvas and target-range labs: there, a plugin mutates ctx.clone and persists it across calls so the next capture builds on the last one. Here the plugin does neither. It never touches ctx.clone , and it doesn't need to remember anything about the DOM from one capture to the next — each pose is a fresh, self-contained render. The afterRender hook centralizes frame collection after capture, using the SVG data URL in ctx.dataURL . An application could also collect result.url after awaiting snapdom() ; this demo uses a plugin callback to keep that bookkeeping in one place. Copy-paste example The plugin factory — it has no idea what a "pose" or a "filmstrip" is, it just collects dataURLs: function frameCollector (onFrame) { let index = 0 return { name: 'frame-collector', afterRender (ctx) { index += 1 onFrame({ index, url: ctx.dataURL }) }, reset () { index = 0 } } } And the usage — capture a pose, read the frame back through the callback: const capturedFrames = [] const collector = frameCollector(frame => { capturedFrames.push(frame.url) }) // runs once per "Capture pose" click, against whatever // pose the sliders are showing at that moment await snapdom(poseScene, { plugins: [collector] }) slider input live style change (no capture) Capture pose snapdom() afterRender (ctx.dataURL) capturedFrames.push() Limits and things to watch The collector has a stateful afterRender hook, so these poses run fresh captures in v3. Resource caches can still be reused. Each SVG data URL stays in memory, so filmstrip size grows with the number and content of the frames. title: Seamless DOM WebGL — The Text You See Isn't Text — SnapDOM Labs
text: ⌕ Overview All labs Live demos Stop motion Paint on a capture Capture stages Target range WebGL Live mirror Seamless DOM Shattered capture Labs / WebGL / Seamless DOM Labs Experiment The text you see isn't text Click into the box below and type. Every glyph you "see" is a WebGL texture rendered from the last SnapDOM capture — the real, editable DOM is invisible on purpose, and updates cross-fade in so nothing ever pops. TL;DR Two DOM elements do the work: a transparent contenteditable proxy that exists only to give the browser a real caret and real keystroke handling, and a hidden source element that mirrors the typed text and is what SnapDOM actually captures. A defineExports plugin feeds each capture into a WebGL renderer that double-buffers two textures and cross-fades between them, so the previous frame can blend into the new one. What you're looking at Clicking into the box and typing feels like a normal text field — you get a blinking caret, text selection, the works. The visible text is displayed through WebGL after the browser renders the captured source. Every glyph on screen is a pixel in a WebGL texture, produced by capturing a completely different, hidden DOM element with SnapDOM and mixing the result into the canvas underneath your cursor. Pick a shader from the dropdown to see the same texture pipeline reused for very different visual effects — the capture and the compositing don't change, only what the fragment shader does with the finished frame. Try it Type, paste, or hit Enter. The caret and selection are real; the letters are not. Shader Faithful Hologram CRT Liquid Kaleidoscope Melt Datamosh Neon Edge Live DOM signal Type here This text is real DOM, but you're seeing it as a WebGL texture kept in sync by SnapDOM. LIVE GPU Hidden DOM double-buffered texture starting… How it works A transparent proxy owns the caret The .input-layer sits visually on top of the WebGL canvas with fully transparent text and background. It exists only to give the browser something to place a real caret on and to receive real keyboard and paste events — its text is transparent while the caret and selection remain visible. Every edit is mirrored to a hidden element On every input event — plus paste, plus Enter (a beforeinput override inserts a literal newline instead of letting contenteditable create a new <div> ) — the proxy's text is copied into the hidden #dom-source element and refresh() runs. refresh() coalesces bursts Same dirty / working loop as the live-mirror demo: if a capture is already in flight when new input arrives, it's flagged dirty and picked up by the loop that's already running, instead of stacking up parallel captures. It captures #dom-source with the seamlessWebgl plugin attached. The plugin exports into the renderer The plugin's defineExports returns a webgl export. Calling it hands the capture's URL to renderer.update(ctx.export.url) instead of returning an image to the page. The idle texture is loaded, not the visible one SeamlessRenderer.update() loads the new capture into whichever of its two textures — current or next — isn't currently on screen, then starts a roughly 110ms blend toward it. The shader mixes, then the effect applies The render loop's fragment shader mixes beforeImage and afterImage by a blend uniform that ramps 0 1 over that window. Whatever shader is selected in the dropdown runs on top of that already-blended result. Why this needed a plugin Same argument as the plain live-mirror demo: SnapDOM's core exports return a finished image and stop — they have no concept of "push this into one of two alternating GPU textures for a crossfade." defineExports is the seam SnapDOM exposes for exactly that: a plugin can register a named export — here, webgl — that does whatever it wants with the render instead of handing back a PNG. What's different here versus the plain live-mirror demo is architectural, not plugin-API related. Splitting the caret-owning element from the capture-source element is what makes the transition look seamless: the visible surface — the canvas — is never waiting on a capture to know what to show. It's always mid-blend between two textures it already has, while the hidden source quietly gets captured again in the background. Copy-paste example The plugin factory — it just forwards a capture's URL to whatever renderer you hand it: function seamlessWebgl (renderer) { let started = 0 let elapsed = 0 return { name: 'seamless-webgl', beforeSnap () { started = performance.now() }, afterRender () { elapsed = performance.now() - started }, defineExports () { return { webgl: async ctx => { const canvas = await renderer.update(ctx.export.url) perfLabel.textContent = `${elapsed.toFixed(0)} ms · texture swapped` return canvas } } } } } And the usage — note this calls the plugin's export through the generic capture.to('webgl') , not a generated capture.toWebgl() helper. Both work; .to(name) is what lets a plugin-defined export be invoked without SnapDOM knowing its name ahead of time: const plugin = seamlessWebgl(renderer) let dirty = false let working = false async function refresh () { dirty = true if (working) return working = true while (dirty) { dirty = false const capture = await snapdom(source, { plugins: [plugin] }) await capture.to('webgl') } working = false } input sync #dom-source refresh() capture.to('webgl') renderer.update() blend 0 1 shader Limits and things to watch The transparent-proxy trick only works cleanly for plain text editing. Anything that needs real DOM selection or formatting UI — rich text, IME composition edge cases — needs more care than this demo attempts; the proxy here deliberately strips formatting down to a literal newline on Enter and plain text on paste. Double-buffering also costs one extra WebGL texture's worth of GPU memory compared to the single-texture live-mirror demo — a deliberate trade for the flicker-free feel, and one that only makes sense when the crossfade is actually the point. title: Target Range — Every Shot Hits the Clone — SnapDOM Labs
text:
⌕ Overview All labs Live demos Stop motion Paint on a capture Capture stages Target range WebGL Live mirror Seamless DOM Shattered capture Labs / Live demos / Target range Labs Experiment Every shot hits the clone A bullet hole is never drawn on the live target in the DOM. A SnapDOM plugin holds onto the clone from the last capture and appends a hit marker to it — every shot re-captures on top of every shot before it. TL;DR SnapDOM's afterRender hook saves the clone it just rendered; afterClone swaps that saved clone back in on the next capture and appends a fresh bullet-hole marker to it. The live target element in the DOM is never touched — the accumulation lives entirely in the plugin's closure. What you're looking at Ten shots, a swaying crosshair, a ring-scoring target — it looks like a canvas-based arcade game. It isn't. The board is a single that gets replaced after every shot with a brand-new snapdom.toPng() result. Nothing in the page's own code remembers where the previous holes landed — that memory lives entirely inside a plugin. Try it Aim, click to fire. The reticle drifts and kicks after every shot, and the drift grows as you run out of ammo. Each shot triggers one real SnapDOM capture — the marker you see appear is the actual exported PNG, not an overlay. 0 Score 10 Shots 0 Best Ready? 10 shots. The reticle sways and kicks with every shot — compensate for the drift. Start Restart Download target The download button uses the that the last snapdom.toPng() call returned, directly — no second capture needed. How it works A hidden source element, never the visible board A 340×340
off-screen holds one SVG target built once from a ring definition. This — not the board you see — is what SnapDOM actually captures. The shot is scored locally, against where the reticle really was On click, the reticle's actual position (after sway and recoil, not the raw mouse position) is converted to a percentage and scored against the ring radii. That { xPct, yPct, color } is handed to plugin.addHit() . addHit() appends a marker to the plugin's saved clone If this is the very first shot, the plugin clones the live source once to start from. Every call after that appends a jagged, randomized torn-paper hole — positioned in percentage coordinates so it survives the clone render round trip — to the clone it already has. snapdom.toPng() runs again, plugin included The demo doesn't touch the target's own DOM at all. It just calls snapdom.toPng(target, { plugins: [plugin] }) again, same as the first shot. afterClone swaps in the saved clone Instead of letting SnapDOM clone the pristine (hole-free) source, the plugin replaces ctx.clone with the clone it's been building — which already carries every hole from every previous shot. afterRender checkpoints the result After SnapDOM finishes rendering, the plugin clones what it just produced and holds onto it as the new baseline for the next shot. The output replaces the board's picture The resulting PNG is inserted directly into the board. The download link just points at that same .src — it becomes the download source without a second capture. Why this needed a plugin SnapDOM v3.x.x can reuse eligible captures, but the accumulated drawing here belongs to the plugin. On each shot, the plugin replaces the new clone with its saved clone and adds the latest mark. Its stateful hooks run on fresh captures. The afterClone and afterRender hooks share the plugin closure. afterClone adds the new mark to savedClone ; afterRender saves the resulting tree for the next call. The plugin owns this drawing state independently of capture reuse. Copy-paste example The plugin factory — the persistent-clone technique works for any "keep building on the last capture" use case, not just bullet holes: function createHitboardPlugin (sourceEl) { let savedClone = null return { name: 'hitboard', afterClone (ctx) { if (savedClone) ctx.clone = savedClone.cloneNode(true) }, afterRender (ctx) { savedClone = ctx.clone.cloneNode(true) }, addHit (xPct, yPct, color) { if (!savedClone) savedClone = sourceEl.cloneNode(true) if (getComputedStyle(savedClone).position === 'static') { savedClone.style.position = 'relative' } const hit = document.createElement('div') hit.style.cssText = ` position: absolute; left: ${xPct}%; top: ${yPct}%; width: 24px; height: 24px; margin: -12px 0 0 -12px; pointer-events: none; ` hit.innerHTML = bulletHoleMarkup(color) savedClone.appendChild(hit) }, reset () { savedClone = null } } } And the usage — score the shot, tell the plugin, capture again: const plugin = createHitboardPlugin(target) function shoot (xPct, yPct) { const { color } = scoreAt(xPct, yPct) plugin.addHit(xPct, yPct, color) return snapdom.toPng(target, { plugins: [plugin] }) } // on restart: plugin = createHitboardPlugin(target) — a fresh closure, // not plugin.reset(), so a stale reference from the finished game can't // leak a hole into the new one. shot addHit() snapdom.toPng() afterClone (restore + append) afterRender (checkpoint) Limits and things to watch addHit() lazily initializes savedClone from the live source the first time it's called, so the plugin never needs to be primed before the first shot. reset() clears it back to null , which lets the very next capture re-clone the pristine source from scratch — a fresh game, fresh holes. That's a simpler shape than Paint Canvas 's skipNext flag: this demo never needs to "skip one capture" mid-stream, because a restart is a hard state reset rather than a stroke boundary the plugin has to detect and route around. title: Capture Stages — a plugin decides how far the pipeline runs
text: ⌕ Overview All labs Live demos Stop motion Paint on a capture Capture stages Target range WebGL Live mirror Seamless DOM Shattered capture Labs / Live demos / Capture stages Labs Experiment Capture stages A capture is a chain: a clone freezes the live DOM at one instant, and a render turns that clone into pixels. Not every consumer needs the whole chain, and the plugin is the one that knows. So it declares it: // Clone only, no image { name: 'my-plugin', needs: 'clone' } // Complete capture (the default) { name: 'my-plugin' } v3 removed a third, shallower stage — needs: 'dom' — which ran the plugin against the live page and took no clone at all. Declaring that removed stage now throws. The stage of a capture is the deepest stage its plugins declare, so one undeclared plugin keeps everything. A capture with no plugins behaves exactly as it always did. Run both stages What the numbers say The clone stage skips render-stage asset embedding and serialization. The saving depends on the page and resources. Compare the timings above; neither stage promises a fixed fraction of a full capture. title: SnapDOM PDF — open-source pdf export
text: Export plugins PDF Vector All plugins PDF reference Full API reference Source · MIT Capture playground Live PDF export Live sample Report A4 ledger Multilingual text Form controls Transparent artwork Page size Fit to content A4 Letter Selectable text Fillable fields Generate PDF Editable source Generated output Nothing generated yet. Previous Next Edit the source, then generate a PDF. Code for this demo Build / Plugins / PDF Official plugin · MIT Export a searchable PDF. Capture a live element, add selectable text and links, and paginate it into a PDF in your browser. Open source PDF is MIT-licensed source inside packages/plugins/pdf . The updated package is not published yet. Run npm run site to try these demos against the local build. How it works The page image plus a PDF text layer The page image is SnapDOM's capture. The plugin places a second, invisible text layer over it using positions derived from SnapDOM's final serialized clone. No headless browser or separate layout engine rebuilds the page. Fidelity The visible result preserves SnapDOM's rendering of gradients, shadows, filters, web fonts and the rest of the captured element. The text layer adds document behaviour without replacing that image. Multilingual text CJK, Cyrillic, Greek, Arabic, Hebrew and emoji carry a /ToUnicode CMap, so selection, search and copy work for every script, whether or not a glyph travels with the file. Pagination Ten page sizes from A6 to tabloid, a custom [width, height] in points, or one page the size of the element. Breaks are pulled up off table rows, list items and figures, and break-before: page is honoured. Headers, footers and page numbers take their room out of the page rather than covering it. Text-form headers/footers and page numbers are real PDF text; Element-form bands are captured images. What reaches the layer Text nodes, input / textarea / select values, open shadow roots, and CSS transforms: rotation and skew go into the text matrix. Passwords are bulleted, never written. What does not Layout-hidden and transparent content is removed. Ambiguous clip, mask and filter geometry is omitted fail-safe. Arbitrary overlap is different: a rectangle or blur can cover pixels without removing the underlying semantic text, so it is not a redaction mechanism. Embedded fonts The faces the page painted with travel inside the file, subset to the glyphs the document actually drew. A ~320 kB face reaches a Latin page as a few kB. Turn on vectorText and eligible runs are painted as real vector glyphs instead of sitting invisible over the raster: crisp at any zoom, and an image-free export of the same page drops from ~420 kB to ~22 kB. Fillable forms A captured form is still a form. Inputs, textareas, checkboxes, radio groups and selects become real AcroForm fields (fillable, tabbable, extractable) carrying their name, value, options, checked state, required and read-only flags, and the accessible label as the tooltip a screen reader speaks. No JavaScript actions, no submit URLs, and a password field is written empty. Encrypted downloads A file that leaves the browser can be AES-256 encrypted on the way out, so the download itself is protected once it is attached and forwarded. Standard security handler revision 6, from the browser's own crypto.subtle , so no cipher code ships in the plugin and RC4 is not offered at any setting. A user password is required: the flavour of "encryption" that opens without asking is refused rather than produced. Identity and determinism Title, author, subject and keywords reach /Info and a mirrored XMP packet; a title also makes viewers show the document's name instead of its filename. Dates are never invented and the trailer /ID is a content hash, so the same unencrypted input produces the same bytes. Progress, cancellation, diagnostics Long exports report progress and take an AbortSignal . Every fidelity trade-off is also a structured diagnostic with a stable code, so a build can gate on "no annotations lost" without parsing console prose. Transparency A capture with alpha carries a Flate /SMask . Flatten it onto a colour to remove the mask. For every image, codec: auto compares JPEG with lossless Flate and keeps the smaller result. The lossless candidate is written in the narrowest colour space that reproduces the pixels exactly, which is one byte per pixel instead of three on the grey or few-coloured regions most page artwork turns out to be. Document features Headings become bookmarks and named destinations. Optional generated contents, repeated table headers, cover/back pages and watermarks make this a document exporter rather than a canvas wrapper. Accessibility structure Tagged output covers headings, prose, lists, tables, sections and figures. The PDF/UA-1 claim is earned, never configured : it is written only when every text operation rode an embedded face, the export is tagged, has a language and displays a title, and no painted image lacks alternative text. When a blocker remains the claim is withheld and the blocker is named . Ships as A minified ES module to ship, an unminified one to read, TypeScript declarations, versioned reference and MIT license. Browser use without a bundler requires an import map for the external SnapDOM peer. Verified by The full Chromium suite parses PDFs back with pdf.js, checks raw bytes (xref offsets, stream lengths, the lot), and one fixture compares the text layer against pixels . A separate gate imports and executes both plugin builds in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit. That is a three-engine API/artifact smoke, not three full layout suites. Quick start Add PDF export to SnapDOM Register the plugin once and every capture gains toPdf() alongside toPng() and toCanvas() . It reuses the existing capture rather than running a second capture engine. import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' import pdf from '@zumer/snapdom-plugins/pdf' snapdom.plugins(pdf()) const shot = await snapdom(document.querySelector( '#report' ), { scale: 2 , dpr: 1 }) const blob = await shot.toPdf({ page: 'a4' , // 'fit' | 'a4' | 'a5' | 'letter' | … margin: 36 , // points header: { left: 'ACME' , right: 'Q3 ledger' }, // real text, or pass an element pageNumbers: true , // or { format, align, size, color } codec: 'auto' , // smaller JPEG or lossless Flate tagged: true , // structure, not a PDF/UA badge download: 'report.pdf' // also downloads it }) On first PDF export, the plugin reads SnapDOM's final serialized clone, not the original live DOM, so real node removal/replacement stays aligned. Page regions are rasterized lazily and cached for later exports. Geometry-preserving final-artifact replacements stay aligned; aspect-preserving width/height scaling is allowed, while incompatible viewBox, root paint/layout or intrinsic-aspect changes fail instead of guessing coordinates. For secrets, remove or replace the node/text; never treat an overlay or blur as redaction. Capture-model options ( formValues , shadow , breakAvoid , outline ) belong in pdf({ ... }) . page 'fit' · one page the size of the element, or a3 / a4 / a5 / a6 / b4 / b5 / letter / legal / tabloid / executive , or [width, height] in points. orientation 'portrait' or 'landscape' . margin Points. 24 . codec auto keeps the smaller JPEG or lossless Flate image. quality Quality of the JPEG candidate. 0.92 . It changes nothing while the lossless candidate wins, which on page artwork is until roughly 0.5 . deflate Deflate the content streams. true . text Emit the selectable layer. true . Turn it off and you get an image-only PDF. links Emit same-document destinations and safe http: , https: , mailto: and tel: annotations. true . image Draw the page image. true . Set false for an image-free PDF that keeps the enabled text, links and structure. Element headers, footers and watermarks are then omitted; cover/back pages keep semantics without their raster. formValues Put input / textarea / select values in the layer. true . shadow Walk open shadow roots. true . breakAvoid Keep page breaks off rows, list items and figures. true . outline Bookmarks from headings; capture-time. true . forms Measure form controls so the export can write fillable fields; capture-time. true . tagged / lang Structure the document and set its spoken language. embedFonts Embed the capture's @font-face binaries, subset to the glyphs the document drew. true . 'full' embeds unsubsetted; false embeds nothing. vectorText Paint eligible runs as real vector glyphs instead of leaving them invisible over the raster. false . RTL and complex scripts stay on the raster. fields Write measured controls as real AcroForm fields. true . false keeps their values in the invisible layer instead. repeatHeaders Repeat a continuing table's thead pixels and text. header A running head across the top of every page. Give it a string or three independent segments, { left, center, right } , each of which can be a function of the page number. Either way it is drawn as real text : selectable, searchable, crisp at any zoom. Pass an element instead and it is captured, for when you need a logo. Either way it takes its height out of the printable area rather than sitting over it. footer The same, along the bottom. pageNumbers true , or { format, align, size, color, font } . Drawn as real PDF text rather than captured, so it stays crisp at any zoom and is searchable like the rest. It sits in the bottom margin, under a footer if there is one. debugText Paint the invisible layer in red, so you can see where it sits. false . cover / toc / back Captured front/back pages and generated linked contents. watermark Text or an element, drawn over every page. encrypt {userPassword, ownerPassword, permissions} . AES-256 (R6). The password is what protects the file; the permission flags are a request a viewer may honour. Needs https or localhost. meta {title, author, subject, keywords, creator, created, modified} /Info and XMP. Dates are written only when you pass them. onProgress ({phase, done, total}) per step, for exports long enough to need a bar. signal An AbortSignal . Aborting rejects between pages with AbortError and produces nothing. onReport The structured diagnostics report once the Blob is finished, with stable warning codes, counts, pages, bytes, fields and annotations. download A filename. Downloads the blob as well as returning it. backgroundColor Flatten at capture, plugin-default or export time. Resolution remains a snapdom(...) concern. Read the complete option, warning and limits reference Open source Included in the SnapDOM monorepo The PDF plugin is available as MIT-licensed source in packages/plugins/pdf . The updated @zumer/snapdom-plugins package is prepared locally and has not been published yet. Read the reference · SnapDOM on GitHub Before you ask Questions Can I use it in something I sell to a client? Yes. The MIT license permits commercial use, modification and redistribution. Keep the license notice with redistributed copies. Is the text really selectable, or is it OCR? It is selectable without OCR. Eligible text is placed from browser geometry in SnapDOM's final serialized clone, so structural exclusions and geometry-preserving replacements stay aligned with the capture. Ambiguous paint effects are omitted fail-safe. Download a sample and copy a paragraph. Is it open source? Yes. The PDF plugin is part of the SnapDOM monorepo under the MIT license. Can I read the code? Yes. Its source, reference and browser test suites live in packages/plugins/pdf in the SnapDOM monorepo. Does it need a server? The exporter itself runs in the browser and returns a Blob ; it does not upload the PDF. SnapDOM may still fetch resources used by the page, or use a proxy if your application configured one. Why is the text raster and not vector? By default the visible pixels preserve SnapDOM's own rendering instead of asking a PDF layout engine to reinterpret the page. Zoom far past the selected capture resolution and you will see pixels. The invisible layer adds selection, search and copy without repainting the type. You can have the other model: vectorText: true paints eligible runs as real glyphs from the embedded fonts, and with image: false the result is a small, fully vector text PDF. It is opt-in because it is a different fidelity promise. RTL and complex scripts are never painted this way, and they stay on the raster. Can the PDF be password protected? Yes. encrypt: { userPassword } writes an AES-256 file, so the download is protected once it is shared. It uses the browser's own crypto, so no cipher code ships in the plugin, and it needs a secure context: https or localhost. Two things it will not do. It does not offer RC4 or the older PDF revisions, whose 40-bit key is broken. And it will not write an empty user password: that produces a file that is encrypted and still opens without asking anyone anything, which is worse than no protection because it looks like some. Permission flags (no printing, no copying) are written when you ask for them, but they are a request a viewer may honour, not a lock. Which browsers? The complete fixture suite is Chromium-only. Both plugin builds must also pass the release artifact smoke in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit. That supports the plugin/API contract in all three; it does not pretend every complex layout has the same three-engine coverage.

title: SnapDOM PDF reference
text: SnapDOM PDF The complete reference for the SnapDOM plugin that adds toPdf() to a capture. The versioned REFERENCE.md shipped beside the module is canonical for that version. The PDF exporter is now MIT-licensed source in the SnapDOM monorepo. The updated plugin package has not been published yet. Installation After the updated package is published, import pdf from @zumer/snapdom-plugins/pdf . For local development, use the monorepo workspace. Bundler import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' import { pdf } from '@zumer/snapdom-plugins/pdf' Browser without a bundler Serve the plugin package with its pdf/src/ tree and a JavaScript MIME type. A global/IIFE SnapDOM script cannot satisfy the plugin's ESM peer import. Requires @zumer/snapdom >=3.0.0 <4 . SnapDOM 3 is the floor. The exporter reads v3's immutable capture metadata, requested export options and pre-decode canvas crops, which 2.x does not expose. The fixture suite runs against the published 3.0.0. Registering The module exports the same pdf factory as default and named export. It does not export a standalone toPdf(element) helper. import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' import pdf, { pdf as namedPdf } from '@zumer/snapdom-plugins/pdf' snapdom.plugins(pdf()) // every later capture const local = await snapdom(el, { plugins: [pdf()] }) // this capture const shot = await snapdom(document.querySelector('#report'), { scale: 2, dpr: 1 }) const blob = await shot.toPdf({ page: 'a4' }) const same = await shot.to('pdf', { page: 'a4' }) Both exports return Promise with type application/pdf . TypeScript declarations add toPdf(options?: PdfExportOptions) to SnapDOM's CaptureResult . Two option moments The PDF model is derived lazily from SnapDOM's final serialized clone on first export, not from the original live DOM. Five options control that model and must be fixed on pdf() before capture: Option Default Meaning formValues true Include visible values of text controls and the selected option. Passwords become bullets. shadow true Walk open shadow roots as the flattened tree. breakAvoid true Measure atomic blocks for pagination. outline true Headings become bookmarks. Use a selector string or false . forms true Measure form controls (kind, name, value, options, geometry, painted style) so the export can write fillable fields. false skips the measurement. Every export option may also be a factory default. A value in toPdf() wins. A capture-time option passed there warns and is ignored. A custom outline selector is evaluated against the final flattened artifact, including matching open-shadow and slotted headings. Page and pagination Option Default Meaning page 'fit' fit ; A3–A6; B4/B5; letter, legal, tabloid, executive; or [width,height] in points. orientation 'portrait' portrait or landscape ; irrelevant to fit . margin 24 Points on all sides; irrelevant to fit . repeatHeaders true Repeat a continuing table's pixels and selectable text. Breaks are pulled off table rows, list items, definitions, figures, blockquotes, replaced content, short leaf blocks and break-inside:avoid content. Declared page breaks are honoured unless they only create an empty page. A block taller than a page still has to split. Only repeats. Its repeated copy has no repeated link annotations, and a header taller than half a page is refused with a warning. Raster Option Default Meaning image true Draw the visible SnapDOM raster. false makes an image-free PDF; Element headers, footers and watermarks are omitted. codec 'auto' Compare JPEG and lossless Flate per image and keep the smaller; or pin jpeg / flate . quality capture / .92 Quality of the JPEG candidate only, taken from the capture when the export does not set one. It reaches nothing when Flate wins, and on ordinary page artwork Flate wins until roughly 0.5 : on a 35-page report 0.92 , 0.8 and 0.6 all produce a byte-identical 11.3 MB, 0.4 gives 10.8 MB and 0.2 gives 10.1 MB. An export whose lowered quality changed nothing says so in the console. scale / dpr on the capture Neither moves a point of geometry, because a PDF has no device to match, so the page box and the text layer are identical whatever they are. They multiply the page image's pixels, and they multiply together : on a 35-page report scale:1, dpr:2 and scale:2, dpr:1 both give 11.3 MB, against 5.1 MB at 1×1 and 24.4 MB at 2×2. dpr defaults to the exporting machine's devicePixelRatio , so pin it if you want the same bytes from a laptop and from CI. backgroundColor capture / null Flatten this PDF export onto a colour instead of carrying alpha. Capture resolution belongs to snapdom(el,{ scale, dpr, width, height }) . Page regions are rasterized lazily and cached on the capture for later exports. A codec, quality or flattening change may still require a new encode; codec:'auto' compares two candidates. When CompressionStream is unavailable, auto uses JPEG and a pinned Flate request warns before falling back. A transparent raster uses a soft mask; flattening usually makes the file smaller. The colour space is earned, not configured Before a region is compressed it is inspected once, and the Flate candidate is written in the narrowest PDF colour space that reproduces those pixels exactly : /DeviceGray when every pixel has r == g == b , an /Indexed palette when the region drew 256 colours or fewer, and /DeviceRGB otherwise. The first two are one byte per pixel instead of three. Page artwork is overwhelmingly one of the first two. Across this project's fixtures, 22 of 29 page regions are grey in every pixel and 23 of 29 fit in a palette, so the effect on real documents is large: a 30-page report drops from 12.4 MB to 8.7 MB, a page of prose by 37%, a typography page by 43%. Regions that genuinely need /DeviceRGB are unchanged, and nothing is approximated to earn the narrowing: the stream inflates back to the original pixels, which the fixture suite asserts by decoding it and comparing pixel for pixel. The narrowing also widens the gap Flate already had over DCT. On every fixture in this project Flate now wins by between 1.7× and 3.6×, which is why quality so often reaches nothing. It is not made to win everywhere. A photographic region is neither grey nor 256 colours, so it narrows to nothing and JPEG can still be the smaller answer. That is exactly why auto still runs the comparison. Text and links Option Default Meaning text true Emit invisible selectable/searchable text. links true Emit external URI and in-document annotations. debugText false Paint the layer red and leave content streams readable. Runs are measured from SnapDOM's final serialized clone, one word at a time. Visible form values, open shadow roots, text transforms and logical bidi text are included. Real removals/replacements from exclude , filter , resolveNode , afterClone , clip , or a geometry-preserving afterRender replacement of the final serialized tree/URL stay aligned. A replacement that changes viewBox, root paint/layout attributes or intrinsic aspect/geometry incompatibly fails instead of producing a misaligned layer. Uniform width/height scaling that preserves aspect is allowed. Layout-hidden and transparent text is excluded. Same-document fragments become PDF destinations. External annotations accept only http: , https: , mailto: and tel: . Missing fragment targets, malformed URLs and other schemes produce no annotation and a warning. Visual occlusion is not redaction. Remove or replace confidential nodes/text. Do not rely on an overlay rectangle, blur or arbitrary overlap: those can hide pixels while leaving semantic text in the serialized document. Ambiguous clipping, masking and filter geometry is omitted fail-safe, so selection may be lost rather than uncertain content exposed. A purely visual afterRender change does not prove semantics changed; an incompatible change to viewBox, root paint/layout or intrinsic aspect fails instead of guessing coordinates. Where no font is embedded, base-14 fonts encode WinAnsi and other scripts use an invisible Type0 font with a /ToUnicode map, so extraction works for every script whether or not a glyph travels. What the file can paint is the next section. Fonts and vector text Option Default Meaning embedFonts true Embed the capture's @font-face binaries and point the text at them. 'full' embeds unsubsetted; false embeds nothing. vectorText false Paint eligible runs as real vector glyphs instead of leaving them invisible over the raster. Embedded fonts The capture has to CARRY its fonts for the export to embed them: pass embedFonts: true to snapdom(…) (the engine option that inlines @font-face ), and the PDF side reads those rules, fetches each face the text actually painted with, and embeds a subset of it: only the glyphs the document drew, renumbered into a dense space. On a Latin page a ~320 kB face travels as a few kB. A face travels once however many styles and pages use it, and the saving is declared per face. The subset renders pixel-identical to the whole font, which the suite asserts by rendering both through pdf.js. It is fail-safe: a TrueType face it cannot subset falls back to a whole embed with an explicit CIDToGIDMap , never a corrupt glyph. CFF/OpenType ( OTTO ) faces are always embedded whole, so 'full' only differs for TrueType. Per run, an embedded face is used only when its own cmap covers every character of that run; a run it cannot carry falls back to the unembedded layer and is counted. System fonts have no bytes a page can hand over and travel by name as before. WOFF unpacks; WOFF2, TrueType collections and faces whose OS/2 fsType forbids embedding are refused with their reason rather than embedded anyway. Text extraction is byte-for-byte identical with and without embedding, because extraction runs off /ToUnicode either way. Vector text By default the visible text is the raster, which is pixel-exact but still pixels. With vectorText: true the exporter paints eligible runs as real vector glyphs from the embedded fonts, so the type is crisp at any zoom and the file is a fraction of the size. That is a different fidelity model from the pixel-exact capture, and it is opt-in for exactly that reason. A run is painted only where no shaping stands between code points and glyphs: left-to-right, in a covering embedded face, with a resolved colour. RTL, complex scripts, uncovered characters and unresolved colours are not painted, because one CID per code point would place their glyphs wrong. Those runs stay on the raster, and in an image-free export they are invisible and reported. image:false, vectorText:true gives a small, fully vector text PDF. Only text and vector furniture travel; borders, checkboxes, background images and any unpaintable run are absent. Measured, the mega fixture is ~22 kB this way against ~420 kB with the raster. image:true, vectorText:true gives the raster plus crisp glyphs painted over it. Larger, but sharp under magnification. Interior glyph positions follow the embedded font's own advances scaled to the run's measured width ( Tz ), not the browser's kerned positions, so a heavily kerned pair can drift sub-pixel from the raster. Extraction is unchanged. Navigation and tagging Option Default Meaning outline true Capture-time bookmarks from headings; see the lifecycle table. tagged true Structure headings, paragraphs, lists, tables, sections and figures. lang DOM / null PDF document language, for example en or es-MX . The PDF/UA-1 claim is earned, never configured There is no option that asserts conformance. The exporter computes eligibility per export and writes the claim only when all of it holds: every text-showing operation on an embedded face, tagged structure present, a document language, a meta.title to display, and no painted image without alternative text. When it does, the XMP carries pdfuaid:part 1 and the report says so ( report.pdfua === true ). When the fonts are clean but a blocker remains, the export does not claim: it names the blockers, so the fix is a line of configuration or markup rather than a guess. Two blockers to know in advance. Fillable fields block the claim, because their editor-facing /DA types in unembedded Helvetica, so a UA-claiming export pairs with fields: false . A painted or role="img" element with no accessible name blocks it too: give it alt , aria-label or title , or alt="" when it is decorative. Links are tagged as /Link structure elements carrying /OBJR references. Fillable form fields Option Default Meaning fields true Emit measured controls as real AcroForm fields that are fillable, tabbable and extractable. false keeps their values in the invisible text layer instead. A captured form should still be a form. Text inputs, textareas, checkboxes, radio groups and selects become widget annotations carrying their DOM name, value, options and checked state. readonly / disabled map to the read-only flag; required and maxlength travel; and the accessible label ( aria-label ,

text: Export plugins PDF Vector All plugins Vector reference Full API reference Source · MIT Capture playground Live Vector export Live sample Component SVG illustration Chart Form controls Generate Vector Editable source Generated output Nothing generated yet. Previous Next Copy to Figma Edit the source, then generate a Vector. Code for this demo Build / Plugins / Vector Official plugin · MIT Export editable vector artwork. Reconstruct supported text and shapes as SVG artwork or copy the captured result into Figma. Open source Vector is MIT-licensed source inside packages/plugins/vector . The updated package is not published yet. Run npm run site to try these demos against the local build. Fidelity See what changes in each format Browsers, SVG and Figma do not support the same effects. The plugin tells you when it had to adapt, rasterize or omit something, and identifies the affected layer. You can review those changes before handing the file to a designer or a client. Exact The destination can reproduce the layer as editable vector content. Adapted The layer remains vector, but an effect was translated to the closest available equivalent. Rasterized or omitted The effect has no usable vector equivalent. The report names the layer and explains what happened. The clearest case is backdrop-filter : frosted glass is a blur of whatever sits behind the panel, and SVG has no way to express that, so the panel arrives as a flat colour. The report names the layer, and the limits list it. Read about fidelity reports How it works Built from the browser's resolved layout Grid, flexbox, sticky positioning and container queries are already resolved on screen. The plugin measures that result instead of trying to implement another CSS layout engine. Editable output Text remains text. Gradients, borders, radii, shadows, transforms, images and DOM hierarchy become vector paint and usable layers. Browser layout Boxes, text lines and baselines are measured from the rendered page, including grid, flexbox, pseudo-elements and open shadow DOM. Private by design The plugin runs in the browser, including authenticated and staging pages. Captures are not uploaded to a server. Tested output 729 checks over 19 fixtures. Fixtures are emitted, rendered and compared against screenshots of the live elements. The whole API Two methods on a SnapDOM capture Register the plugin on a capture and it gains toVector() and toFigma() , alongside toPng() and toCanvas() . The only option is exclude . import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' import vector from '@zumer/snapdom-plugins/vector' const shot = await snapdom(document.querySelector( '#plan-card' ), { plugins: [vector()] }) const svg = await shot.toVector() // standalone SVG, no foreignObject, text is text await shot.toFigma() // on the clipboard: paste it into Figma Read the reference Where it goes An SVG file, or a paste into Figma Both come from the same capture of the page, and neither needs a server or an install. Flat SVG shot.toVector() Standalone SVG with editable text and native shapes. Open it in Illustrator, Inkscape, Penpot, Figma, a browser, a printer or a plotter. Figma shot.toFigma() Copies the capture in Figma's own paste format. Paste it into a Figma file and you get frames, editable text, gradients, shadows and images, with nothing installed. The format is undocumented, so if a Figma release breaks it, the SVG route keeps working while we update. Open source Included in the SnapDOM monorepo The Vector plugin is available as MIT-licensed source in packages/plugins/vector . The updated @zumer/snapdom-plugins package is prepared locally and has not been published yet. Read the reference · SnapDOM on GitHub Before you ask Questions Is this a tracer? Does it vectorise the pixels? No. Nothing is traced and nothing is recognised. Every box, line and baseline is read from the live layout, and every fill is parsed from the CSS that produced it. A tracer cannot tell you the second stop of a gradient; this hands you its colour and position. Will my page come into Figma perfect? No, and any tool that says otherwise is one you will stop trusting on the third capture. Some things have no Figma equivalent at all: a colour-matrix filter, OpenType feature settings, per-range baseline shift. The difference here is that you get the list, per node, before you paste. Do I need a Figma plugin? No. toFigma() copies the capture and you paste it into Figma. The flat SVG opens in Illustrator, Inkscape, Penpot and any browser too, which is why this is not a Figma product with a lock-in problem. Does anything leave the machine? No. The engine runs in your page, and the copy for Figma goes through your own clipboard. For a lot of teams that is a legal requirement. Which browsers? Chromium today. Everything is measured there and the pixel baselines were recorded there. We have not run it against Firefox or WebKit, so we are not claiming them. What if it does not work for my page? Send us the page. A reproducible case helps improve fidelity, and the samples above are there so you can check the output on pages like yours first.

title: snapdom-vector documentation
text: snapdom-vector A SnapDOM plugin. Register it on a capture and that capture gains toVector() , a standalone SVG, and toFigma() , a copy you paste into Figma. This page is the whole reference. Getting started The Vector plugin and its internal SVD format live in packages/plugins/vector under the MIT license. The updated plugin package has not been published yet. SnapDOM 3 is a peer dependency; it is not bundled in. import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' import vector from '@zumer/snapdom-plugins/vector' const shot = await snapdom(document.querySelector( '#plan-card' ), { plugins: [vector()] }) const svg = await shot.toVector() // a standalone SVG string await shot.toFigma() // on the clipboard: paste it into Figma Nothing runs on a server and nothing is uploaded. Everything happens in the page you are already looking at, which is the point: the component worth capturing is usually behind a login. Registering Register it per capture . Registering it globally costs you something, so here are both forms and the reason to prefer the first: // this capture only, and the one to use await snapdom(el, { plugins: [vector()] }) // every capture in the page snapdom.plugins(vector()) A plugin with render hooks suspends SnapDOM's burst optimisation on the captures it runs on, because burst answers with a memoized URL without re-entering the capture pipeline, and then there is no clone for this engine to read. Registered per capture, that cost lands on the captures that asked for it. Registered globally, it lands on all of them, including the toPng() in your hot path. Both methods throw if the captured element has no layout box (an element with display: none has nothing to measure), and if the capture carries no clone, which happens when burst: true was forced on the snapdom() call. Leave burst unset. The captured element must still be connected, with its styles available, when you export. Everything about the capture stays on the snapdom() call. scale , dpr , backgroundColor and the rest are read before the plugin runs, so there is no second set of names for them here. exclude Option Default exclude none A CSS selector, a predicate (element) => boolean , or an array of either. Matching elements and their subtrees are left out of the vector output, text and layer names included. It is the only option. Give it to vector({ exclude }) as the default for every export from that capture, or to a single toVector() or toFigma() call, where it wins for that call. const shot = await snapdom(el, { plugins: [vector({ exclude: '.no-print' })] }) const svg = await shot.toVector({ exclude: [ '.no-print' , (node) => node.dataset.private === 'true' ] }) SnapDOM's own exclude on the snapdom() call also applies: anything it leaves out of the capture never reaches the vector output. toVector() shot.toVector(options?) → Promise <string> A standalone SVG string. No foreignObject , anywhere. An SVG with a foreignObject in it is an HTML document wearing an SVG hat, and every vector tool opens it empty. Here a rectangle is a <rect> and a line of text is a <text> . The file opens in Illustrator, Inkscape, Penpot, Figma and any browser. The browser breaks the lines and the SVG only draws them. A block that occupies more than one line becomes one <text> per visual line, each at its measured baseline, so no editor re-wraps your paragraph differently. Gradients, borders, radii, shadows, transforms, clips and images become native SVG paint. -webkit-text-stroke is a real stroke, and background-clip: text becomes the text's own fill. textLength is written only when a font binary travels with the file. Pinning a line to a width measured with your font, in a viewer that substituted another one, squeezes the glyphs. Native form controls are reconstructed at Chromium's measured proportions from their kind, state and accent colour, and each one is declared as a reconstruction. The file is self-describing : the approximations are written into an XML comment under the <svg> tag, so a file that travels without its report cannot exist. toFigma() shot.toFigma(options?) → Promise <void> Puts the capture on the clipboard in Figma's own paste format. Paste into a Figma file and you get frames, editable text, gradients, shadows, borders and images, with nothing installed. It resolves once the clipboard holds the copy. button.addEventListener( 'click' , async () => { await shot.toFigma() toast( 'Copied. Paste it into Figma.' ) }) Call it from a user action, on https or localhost. It uses the async clipboard API, and browsers only let a page the user is interacting with write to the clipboard. Outside a secure context it rejects with a message that says so. letter-spacing survives , which Figma's SVG importer cannot do: measured, a 376.8px line of text arrives at 449px through the SVG route, 50px of that from ignored tracking. Nodes whose paint the paste format cannot spell are drawn as vector artwork and carried as an image, unless they hold text, which stays editable. Effects that read what is underneath a node ( mix-blend-mode , backdrop-filter ) arrive unblended. The format is Figma's, and it is undocumented. Figma can change it in any release, with no error; the only symptom is a paste that does nothing. If that happens, toVector() and Figma's SVG import keep working while we update. Diagnostics Every approximation (a conic gradient drawn as wedges, a shadow spread folded into a blur, a filter a destination cannot run) is printed to the console under [snapdom-vector] , grouped by code with a count and up to three distinct messages, so four hundred identical warnings come out as one line and a count. The codes are stable and greppable, and toVector() also writes the list into the SVG. A diagnostic that says something will be lost in the destination (the SVG is exactly right in a browser, and Figma runs only part of it) is a warning about where the file is going, not a degradation of the file. What reaches the output, and what does not The engine walks the clone SnapDOM already resolved, which is why membership in the tree is not an argument here. In: Pseudo-elements ( ::before , ::after , ::first-letter ) as real nodes with real boxes, with counters and quotes resolved. Shadow DOM , flattened, so slotted content appears once, at the slot. Icon fonts resolved by ligature, and inline <svg> carried as vector with its element ids namespaced per instance. Images from currentSrc , so srcset resolves to what was actually shown, with object-fit and object-position applied. An SVG source is inlined as vector, not rasterized. Scroll offsets , applied, and overflow clipping as a real clip. <canvas> and <video> , as bitmaps. A tainted canvas is omitted with a reason rather than throwing. In-flight animations , at the values of the frame that was captured. Out: Anything exclude named, and anything SnapDOM itself excludes. display: none , visibility: hidden , and content clipped away by an overflow ancestor. The value inside a native control. The text in an <input> , the chosen <option> of a <select> and a placeholder are painted by the browser itself and no CSS property describes them. The widget's frame, border and background are drawn. Cross-origin iframes. The frame becomes a placeholder. Closed shadow roots , which are unreadable by anyone. Limits Written down because you will meet them, and meeting them here is better than meeting them in front of a client. Chromium. Everything is measured there and the pixel baselines were recorded there. Other engines are not tested, and we do not claim them. No font binary travels. The output names the family and the face; it does not embed the file. So a viewer without your font substitutes one. A system font keyword is not a font name. Text painted by -apple-system or system-ui cannot tell any destination which face to load. Auto Layout is not inferred. Everything lands positioned. A frame you can move is not a frame that reflows, and guessing wrong at the layout is worse than not guessing. backdrop-filter does not survive. Frosted glass is a blur of whatever sits behind the panel, and neither SVG nor Figma can say that about an arbitrary backdrop. The panel arrives as a flat colour, and the diagnostics name it. A conic gradient becomes 128 flat wedges plus a small disc capping the apex. SVG has no conic paint server. Shadow spread is approximate. feMorphology 's kernel is rectangular, so the spread corners are. 3D transforms are flattened to their 2D projection, with a diagnostic. Figma has no colour-matrix effect , so filter: saturate(…) and its relatives have no equivalent there. They are named, with the CSS verbatim, rather than dropped quietly. The capture is one subtree, one viewport, one moment. No page-wide capture, no responsive variants, no component variants inferred from a static picture. Something here wrong or missing? Tell us . The documentation is part of what you bought.

This reference covers SnapDOM v3.x.x. Maintaining an older project? Read the archived v2 documentation . Quick start API reference What is SnapDOM SnapDOM is a browser capture engine for web interfaces. It captures a DOM subtree with its styles and assets into a reusable result. The core exports SVG, PNG, JPG, WebP, canvas and blobs, and reports capture geometry. Plugins add HTML, text or JSON context, annotated element maps and image-based PDFs from that state, or record new captures as GIF or video. Documentation sections API reference — methods & exporters Options — every capture option Plugins — extend the pipeline Cache & preCapture — performance Quick start Capture any DOM element to PNG in one line: import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom'; const img = await snapdom.toPng(document.querySelector('#card')); document.body.appendChild(img); Reusable capture (one clone, multiple exports): const result = await snapdom(document.querySelector('#card')); await result.toPng(); // → HTMLImageElement await result.toSvg(); // → SVG as Image await result.download({ format: 'jpg', filename: 'card.jpg' }); Installation NPM / Yarn npm i @zumer/snapdom@latest yarn add @zumer/snapdom@latest CDN <!-- Minified build --> <script src="https://unpkg.com/@zumer/snapdom@latest/dist/snapdom.js"></script> <!-- Minified ES Module build --> <script type="module"> import { snapdom } from "https://unpkg.com/@zumer/snapdom@latest/dist/snapdom.mjs"; </script> Build outputs Variant File Use case ESM (tree-shakeable) dist/snapdom.mjs Bundlers (Vite, webpack), import IIFE (global) dist/snapdom.js Browser script tag; exposes window.snapdom . No CommonJS build. Plugin registry import. The subpath shares the core runtime and registry: import { registerPlugins } from '@zumer/snapdom/plugins'; Capture flow A capture freezes the subtree; exports then read that captured state. The work is split into these steps: Stage What happens Clone Deep clone with styles, Shadow DOM, iframes. Leave nodes out with exclude . Styles & Pseudo Inline ::before / ::after as elements, resolve counter() / counters() . Images & Backgrounds Fetch and inline external images/backgrounds as data URLs. Fonts Embed the webfonts the capture uses by default. Render icon-font glyphs through the icon path. SVG Wrap clone in <foreignObject> , serialize to data:image/svg+xml . Export Return the SVG, rasterize to PNG/JPG/WebP/canvas, create a blob, or run a plugin export. Plugins can use the clone without rendering by declaring needs: 'clone' . Image exports require 'render' , the default. Hooks and custom outputs are covered in the plugins guide . Usage patterns Pattern When to use snapdom(el) Reusable — one clone many exports (PNG + JPG + download). snapdom.toPng(el) Shortcut — single export, less code. See the full API reference for every method and the options reference for everything you can pass.
