How-to / Basics / Convert HTML to PNG How-To Recipe How to convert HTML to PNG in JavaScript Three patterns: append the image to the page, download it as a file, or get a Blob to upload. Pick the one that fits your use case and copy the snippet. TL;DR const img = await snapdom.toPng(element); — that returns an HTMLImageElement . Append it, download it, or convert to a Blob with snapdom.toBlob(element, { format: 'png' }) if you need a PNG Blob to upload. Step 1 — Install npm install @zumer/snapdom@latest Or load it from a CDN if you don't use a bundler: < script type= "module" > import { snapdom } from "https://unpkg.com/@zumer/snapdom@latest/dist/snapdom.mjs" ; </ script > Pattern 1 — Append the PNG to the page Useful for quick previews and demos. snapdom.toPng returns an HTMLImageElement , ready to insert anywhere in the DOM: import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' ; const img = await snapdom. toPng (document. querySelector ( '#card' )); document.body. appendChild (img); Pattern 2 — Download the PNG as a file SnapDOM ships with a one-liner that triggers the browser's download flow: const result = await snapdom (document. querySelector ( '#card' )); await result. download ({ format: 'png' , filename: 'card' }); If you need more control, build the download yourself with a Blob and an anchor tag: const blob = await snapdom. toBlob (document. querySelector ( '#card' ), { format: 'png' }); const url = URL. createObjectURL (blob); const a = document. createElement ( 'a' ); a.href = url; a.download = 'card.png' ; a. click (); URL. revokeObjectURL (url); Pattern 3 — Upload the PNG to a server Capture the element to a Blob, wrap it in FormData , and POST it to your endpoint: const blob = await snapdom. toBlob (document. querySelector ( '#card' ), { format: 'png' }); const form = new FormData (); form. append ( 'file' , blob, 'card.png' ); const response = await fetch ( '/api/upload' , { method: 'POST' , body: form, }); const { url } = await response. json (); console . log ( 'Uploaded to' , url); This is the same pattern you'd use to generate dynamic og:image share cards — capture the rendered card client-side, upload to a CDN, return the URL. Try the three patterns live Same element, three buttons — append the PNG, download it, or produce the upload-ready Blob: HTML PNG Gradients, borders & shadows Rounded corners, a dashed border, a gradient — ready to capture together. ⚡ Even this shadow Append PNG Download Get Blob The result will appear here. Bonus — Get a Base64 / data URL If you specifically need a base64 string (e.g. to email or embed inline), call toPng and read the src of the returned image: const img = await snapdom. toPng (document. querySelector ( '#card' )); const dataUrl = img.src; // "data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgo…" High-DPI / retina output SnapDOM picks up the device's devicePixelRatio automatically through the dpr option, so retina screens already get sharp output without configuration. Override it with dpr when you want a fixed pixel density (e.g. exporting a 2× asset on a non-retina machine): const img = await snapdom. toPng (el, { dpr: 2 }); scale multiplies the captured size when no explicit width or height is set. Use scale when you want a larger image; use dpr when you want the same logical size at higher pixel density. They can be combined: const img = await snapdom. toPng (el, { dpr: 2 , // retina pixel density scale: 1.5 , // zoom 1.5× backgroundColor: '#ffffff' , }); Frequently asked questions Can I convert HTML to PNG without a server? Yes. SnapDOM runs in the browser and does not need a screenshot server. Its SVG foreignObject pipeline uses the browser's renderer; fonts and images may still require network requests. What if I need JPG or WebP instead of PNG? Use snapdom.toJpg(el, { quality: 0.9 }) or snapdom.toWebp(el, { quality: 0.9 }) . The API surface is identical, only the output format changes. How do I render custom fonts correctly? SnapDOM v3.x.x defaults to embedFonts: 'auto' , which embeds used web fonts when their files are accessible. Use localFonts or excludeFonts when you need more control. Can I exclude some elements from the capture? Yes. Pass { exclude: ['.skip-me'] } with a list of CSS selectors, or { exclude: node => … } for a predicate that returns true for nodes to omit. What about converting HTML to PDF? Use the MIT pdf plugin. Its toPdf() method returns a PDF Blob with selectable text, pagination and links. The updated package is prepared locally; see the PDF reference for installation and examples. Does it handle Shadow DOM and Web Components? Yes. SnapDOM walks open Shadow DOM trees during cloning, and preserves their rendered styles subject to the same resource and browser limits as other captures. TL;DR SnapDOM needs a browser DOM. Use a client component for the ref and event handler, then import SnapDOM inside the handler. This keeps capture code out of server rendering. 1. Install npm install @zumer/snapdom@latest Run the capture in a browser event handler after the component has hydrated. 2. App Router — client component Create a client component that owns the ref and capture logic. 'use client' defines a client boundary, but client components may still be prerendered. Importing SnapDOM inside the click handler keeps that import in the browser. // app/capture/CaptureCard.tsx 'use client' ; import { useRef } from 'react' ; export default function CaptureCard () { const cardRef = useRef <HTMLDivElement>( null ); async function handleCapture () { if (!cardRef.current) return ; const { snapdom } = await import ( '@zumer/snapdom' ); const img = await snapdom. toPng (cardRef.current, { scale: 2 }); document.body. appendChild (img); } return ( < div > < div ref={cardRef} className= "card" > < h3 >Hello SnapDOM</ h3 > < p >Captured from a Next.js client component.</ p > </ div > < button onClick={handleCapture}>Capture</ button > </ div > ); } Try it live This is what CaptureCard does after hydration, running on this page. Capture Download The captured PNG will appear here. 3. Use it from a server page Server components can render this client component as a child. The 'use client' boundary allows its event handler and ref; the dynamic import inside the handler runs when the user captures: // app/capture/page.tsx import CaptureCard from './CaptureCard' ; export default function Page () { return ( < main > < h1 >SnapDOM in Next.js</ h1 > < CaptureCard /> </ main > ); } 4. Alternative — dynamic import (lazy load) The handler above already loads SnapDOM on demand. You can also load the entire capture component dynamically with SSR disabled. Put this dynamic() call inside a client component: // app/capture/CaptureLazy.tsx 'use client' ; import dynamic from 'next/dynamic' ; export const CaptureCard = dynamic (() => import ( './CaptureCard' ), { ssr: false , loading: () => < p >Loading capture tool…</ p >, }); Your server page then imports CaptureCard from this wrapper. In the pages router ( pages/capture.tsx ) there's no 'use client' directive and no restriction — ssr: false works directly in the page file. 5. Bonus — dynamic OG / share images SnapDOM is great for generating share cards on the fly when the user clicks "share". Capture the rendered card to a Blob, upload it to your CDN, and use that URL as the og:image for the share link: async function share () { if (!cardRef.current) return ; const { snapdom } = await import('@zumer/snapdom'); const blob = await snapdom. toBlob (cardRef.current, { scale: 2 , format: 'png' }); const form = new FormData (); form. append ( 'file' , blob, 'share.png' ); await fetch ( '/api/upload' , { method: 'POST' , body: form }); } For server-rendered OG images that don't need a real browser, Vercel's @vercel/og is a different tool — see the FAQ below. Common gotchas "window is not defined" / "document is not defined" errors Import SnapDOM inside a browser event handler, as shown above, or load the capture component with dynamic(() => import('./CaptureCard'), { ssr: false }) from a client component. A 'use client' directive alone does not prevent prerendering. The captured image is blank in production but works in dev Check that the target is mounted, has a nonzero size and contains the expected data. Wait for layout-changing assets such as fonts. SnapDOM v3.x.x embeds used web fonts with embedFonts: 'auto' by default; a blank capture can have causes beyond font loading. Should I use SnapDOM or @vercel/og for OG images? Different tools. @vercel/og renders Satori-compatible JSX on the server (no real browser, no full CSS). SnapDOM runs client-side in a real browser and captures the rendered DOM, including supported pseudo-elements, custom fonts and open Web Components. Use @vercel/og when the card is fully described in JSX and you don't need real browser fidelity. Use SnapDOM when you want to capture a piece of your live UI with its current browser layout. Can I run SnapDOM in a server action? No. Server actions run in Node.js without a real DOM. Use Puppeteer or Playwright if you need server-side screenshots, and SnapDOM client-side. Cross-origin images break the capture Pass a CORS proxy via { useProxy: 'https://your-proxy.example.com/' } . SnapDOM will fetch external images through the proxy and inline them as data URLs. Does it work with Turbopack? SnapDOM has an ES module entry and no native runtime dependencies. Keep its import and capture calls inside the browser boundary when using Turbopack or Webpack. When to use which Choose SnapDOM when… You use modern CSS: variables, ::before/::after , gradients, transforms, line-clamp. Your UI uses Web Components or Shadow DOM. You need to embed custom fonts in the output. You need plugins for transformations or exports such as HTML, structured context, maps, ASCII or PDF images. You care about bundle size and zero dependencies. Keep html2canvas when… Your existing captures meet your requirements and migration would add work without a measured benefit. Compare representative output before changing libraries. Check the issue tracker for known problems affecting your content, then measure both implementations. Same task, side by side Capturing #card as a PNG and inserting the resulting image into the page: html2canvas import html2canvas from 'html2canvas' ; const canvas = await html2canvas (document. querySelector ( '#card' )); const img = new Image (); img.src = canvas. toDataURL ( 'image/png' ); document.body. appendChild (img); SnapDOM import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' ; const img = await snapdom. toPng (document. querySelector ( '#card' )); document.body. appendChild (img); SnapDOM returns the HTMLImageElement ready to be appended — no manual toDataURL call. If you do need a canvas, call snapdom.toCanvas(el) instead. Migration notes Common operations have equivalents, but image return types and option meanings differ. These examples preserve the requested output format: html2canvas SnapDOM html2canvas(el) snapdom.toCanvas(el) canvas.toDataURL('image/png') (await snapdom.toPng(el)).src canvas.toDataURL('image/jpeg', 0.9) (await snapdom.toJpg(el, { quality: 0.9 })).src canvas.toBlob(cb, 'image/png') await snapdom.toBlob(el, { format: 'png' }) { scale: 2 } { dpr: 2 } { backgroundColor: '#fff' } { backgroundColor: '#fff' } { ignoreElements: skip } { exclude: skip } — (not supported) { embedFonts: true } For a Canvas consumer, start with this change and compare the output: // Before import html2canvas from 'html2canvas' ; const canvas = await html2canvas (el, { scale: 2 }); // After import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' ; const canvas = await snapdom. toCanvas (el, { dpr: 2 }); Frequently asked questions Why does html2canvas not render my Shadow DOM? Shadow DOM support depends on the capture implementation. SnapDOM walks accessible open Shadow roots, copies resolved styles and renders the clone through SVG <foreignObject> . Closed roots are not accessible through the standard DOM API. html2canvas doesn't render web fonts correctly, what do I use? First check that your fonts load before capture. SnapDOM v3.x.x uses embedFonts: 'auto' by default to embed used web fonts in the SVG. The font files must be accessible to the page; test the resulting image in your target browser. html2canvas is slow on large DOMs, is there a faster alternative? SnapDOM uses a different rendering path and can reuse eligible captures in v3. The gain depends on the DOM, assets and capture pattern. Use the live benchmark above and compare your own elements before choosing. Is html2canvas still maintained in 2026? This page compares html2canvas 1.4.1 . For current maintenance status, check its releases and issue tracker . A release date alone does not establish whether a library meets your capture requirements. TL;DR SnapDOM captures an element already rendered in the user browser. Playwright is best for cross-browser automation, end-to-end tests and server-side screenshots. Different tools for different execution models Requirement SnapDOM Playwright Runs in an existing web app Yes Via automation Needs server infrastructure No Usually Capture arbitrary URLs No Yes Controlled browser engine User browser Yes Element export button Direct Network workflow Choose SnapDOM when The element already exists in the user’s DOM. The export should work client-side without uploading private UI. You need SVG, PNG, JPEG, WebP, Canvas or Blob from one capture. Choose Playwright when You must render without an active user browser. You need navigation, authentication automation or full-page URL screenshots. Output must come from a controlled browser build. No. It replaces client-side element capture, not remote-page rendering or browser automation. Can both be used together? Yes. Playwright can load a page that uses SnapDOM, though direct browser screenshots may be simpler in an automated workflow. text: ⌕ Overview HTML-to-image libraries Live benchmark Head to head vs html2canvas vs html-to-image vs dom-to-image vs modern-screenshot Architecture vs Puppeteer vs Playwright Compare / Live benchmark Live benchmark Run the comparison on your own machine Nothing on this page is pre-recorded. Pick a scene, pick the libraries, and every number below is measured in your browser, right now — using the same adapters, the same scenes and the same pixel oracle the SnapDOM repository uses for its own benchmarks. How to read it One output stage for everyone. Every library is timed through to a PNG data URL. Comparing an SVG URL with a PNG would omit rasterization and encoding from one side. Cold and repeat are different numbers. First capture builds a new element for every run. Repeat captures the same element again. Compare both columns because reuse can change the timing and ranking. Defaults, scale 1. This lab loads SnapDOM from @latest and uses fixed competitor versions. No library is configured for advantage. SnapDOM runs with burst: false in every scene except Polling , so its memoization is not compared against everyone else's full pipeline. The table does not know who should win. Rows are sorted by measured time and the fastest is highlighted, whoever it is. On some scenes that is not SnapDOM. Absolute milliseconds depend on your CPU, your browser and how busy the machine is. The ratios are the part worth quoting. Scene Run benchmark Copy results as markdown The page is held still while a run is in progress. A library that clones the whole document crops at viewport-relative coordinates, so scrolling mid-capture can change the region it captures. Library First capture Repeat vs fastest Output Differs from SnapDOM The last column is the share of pixels that differ from SnapDOM's capture beyond a per-channel tolerance — not a correctness verdict, since SnapDOM is only the reference because it is the library this page ships. Small differences may come from antialiasing or font rasterization, but can also reveal a real defect. A large number means the two libraries did not render the same thing, and the gallery below shows which: milliseconds cannot tell a fast capture from a fast capture of the wrong thing . Every row must also produce the same output size , and must actually paint something. A row tagged not comparable rendered at a different resolution, and one tagged blank output returned a correctly-sized image with nothing in it — in both cases the milliseconds are measuring the wrong thing. Treat those rows as bug reports, not results. What each library actually produced. Click one to open it full size — speed is only half the comparison, and this is the other half. Capability matrix, verified by pixels Feature tables are usually copied from READMEs. This one is not: it captures a fixture where each capability paints its own marker colour, then counts those pixels in the output. A library "supports" something here only if the colour survived the round trip. It starts by proving the oracle can say no — the same fixture is built with every capability removed, and all six must read absent. A checker that cannot fail is a checker that means nothing. Run the capability matrix The oracle self-test runs first. Cells report behaviour with defaults . Some libraries pass more of these once configured — html2canvas, for instance, handles conic gradients with foreignObjectRendering: true . Results also vary by engine: run this page in Safari and Firefox and compare. What this page cannot tell you It is one machine — yours. A run on a busy laptop, in a background tab, or with an extension injecting stylesheets will move every row. Run it twice. Competitors load from a CDN. Anything jsDelivr cannot serve you shows up as a row that could not load, not as a win. Speed is not fidelity. A library that skips shadow DOM has less work to do. Read the output gallery and the capability matrix alongside the milliseconds, never instead of them. These are synthetic scenes. They were chosen because they isolate a cost — per-node work, author-stylesheet scanning, shadow traversal, large-output raster — not because they are your page. The same scenes run in the repository as __tests__/category.*.benchmark.js . Compare library versions, browser, scene and capture mode when investigating a difference.
